team.name: Max Feinstein
team.blurb: A specialist in postmodern literature and critical methodology, redefining competitive discourse through rigor.
team.depth:
About me
My name is Max Feinstein, and I am a sophomore at The Altamont School in Birmingham, Alabama. Debate is my primary academic interest, and I enjoy rounds where I learn new things. Subjectivity shift is real!

Outside of debate, I play ECNL and varsity soccer for Altamont (Go Knights!) and have been playing piano, electric guitar, and acoustic guitar for quite a while. I enjoy reading extensively in both philosophy and other literature critical literature and am an avid NBA fan—especially of the San Antonio Spurs. I value collaborative learning environments and enjoy working with teammates and friends to create new arguments and strategies.

Debate Background & Argument Interests
I specialize primarily in Kritikal and Phil/tricks debate. For the k I am most comfortable engaging with postmodern literature though fine for all k lit.

Strategically, I am drawn to arguments that emphasize methodological and ideological evaluation, framing disputes, and real impact calculus with different weighing metric indicts rather than purely empirical cost-benefit analysis.

Email me at feinsteinm29@altamontschool.org.

faq.a: The AFF (Affirmative) supports the resolution by arguing that its central claim is morally or practically true. They carry the burden of proof, using a framework of values and contentions to demonstrate why the resolution should be adopted.

The NEG (Negative) opposes the resolution by refuting the Affirmative’s arguments or providing independent reasons why the resolution is harmful. They aim to create enough doubt or counter-evidence to prove that the resolution should be rejected.
LD is a one-on-one debate format focusing on philosophical values and criteria. It traditionally clashes on moral imperatives, though modern 'circuit' LD includes policy-style plans and kritiks.
Policy debate involves two-on-two teams debating a government's course of action. It is highly technical, evidence-intensive, and focuses on pragmatism and structural outcomes.
Flowing is the specialized form of note-taking used by debaters to track the evolution of every argument throughout a round, usually organized in columns by speech.

A Kritik is a type of argument that challenges the philosophical, ethical, or linguistic assumptions of an opponent's case or the resolution itself. It often focuses on systemic issues like capitalism, racism, or biopower.

A Counterplan is a competitive alternative to the Affirmative plan proposed by the Negative. To win, the Neg must prove the CP is better than the plan and that you cannot or should not do both (mutual exclusivity).

Topicality is a procedural argument made by the Negative claiming the Affirmative plan does not fall within the definition of the resolution. It is a 'voting issue' because it affects fairness and education.

Theory arguments are meta-debates about the rules of the round. Debaters use theory to claim that an opponent's specific style or argument (like 'multiple conditional counterplans') is unfair and should be penalized.
Tricks are a subset of LD arguments that rely on hidden logical 'spikes' or paradoxes designed to be missed by an opponent, leading to an automatic win if conceded.
Spreading (speed reading) is a technique used to deliver arguments at a high rate of words-per-minute to maximize the amount of evidence and logic introduced in a limited speech time.
Disclosure is the practice of posting your evidence and case citations on the official Wiki (Tabroom/Opencaselist) before a round to allow for better-prepared, higher-level technical clashes.

A permutation (perm) is an Affirmative test of competitiveness against a Negative counterplan or kritik. It argues that the plan and the alternative can be done simultaneously, meaning the alternative isn't a reason to vote Neg.

An impact turn is when you argue that the 'bad' thing your opponent claims will happen is actually a 'good' thing (or vice-versa). For example, arguing that 'economic growth' is actually harmful due to environmental destruction.
